title: Early-career hiring fell in the most AI-exposed industry-state markets after ChatGPT
source_unit: Census CES Working Paper 26-27 using matched employer-employee administrative data and Quarterly Workforce Indicators tabulations
geography: United States; industry-state cells, early-career workers ages 22-24, older workers, and AI-exposure quintiles

observations.period: ChatGPT introduction through 2025 Q2; paper published April 2026

denominator.unit: industry-state cell and worker-age-group administrative-data analysis

early_career_employment.value: regression-adjusted employment declined 12% in the most AI-exposed quintile over the 10 quarters after ChatGPT's introduction

hiring.value: the decline in hires was the primary cause of the subsequent employment decline

comparison.value: employment in less AI-exposed industries remained stable over the comparison period

recovery.value: hiring largely recovered by early 2025, but from a smaller employment base

earnings.value: earnings growth for early-career workers in the most exposed industries slowed slightly relative to less exposed industries

alternative_explanations.value: COVID-era trend shifts, remote work, educational attainment, and monetary-policy shocks may explain part of the pattern but do not explain the rapid relative hiring decline in the most exposed firms

observations.method: The author uses matched employer-employee administrative data, detailed industry-state AI-exposure cells, event studies, triple differences, local projections, and historical decomposition to compare early-career and older workers.
observations.uncertainty: This is a Census CES working paper and not a Census Bureau endorsement. AI exposure is an industry-state classification rather than verified firm-level AI use; the timing is consistent with an effect after ChatGPT but the paper also identifies earlier trend shifts and other macro explanations.
observations.subgroup: Early-career workers ages 22-24 compared with older workers in the same industries; effects vary by industry exposure and the source does not establish the full experience by race, gender, education, family resources, occupation, or local place.
observations.counterinterpretation: Hiring can respond to demand, interest rates, remote work, education, sector composition, or other post-pandemic changes. Lower entry hiring is not automatically permanent displacement; later recovery from a smaller base may represent delayed entry, sorting, scarring, or substitution, which this record does not resolve.

related_sources.claim: The official paper provides the QWI construction, event-study comparisons, exposure definition, and alternative-explanation tests.

boundary: This record adds an entry-to-work AI-exposure pathway distinct from firm adoption and college-major exposure. It does not establish individual automation, permanent displacement, lifetime scarring, or the distribution of gains and losses across households.
